Feature importance and deep extrapolation

  • Why profiles can become odd below five bins
  • How XGBoost feature importance works
  • What drives shallow versus deep predictions?
  • Inspecting individual profile shapes
  • What this supports, and what to check next
  • Reproduction and checks

The lowest observed density bin is the strongest individual input. Depth below that bin and target height above terrain also matter. In a small paired-site sample, depth, terrain height, and time features contribute more strongly to predictions at five or more bins down. This explains model behavior; it does not establish the biological cause of a profile shape or prove that a particular feature causes prediction error.

Why profiles can become odd below five bins

The saved with-AGL model’s raw-density validation R² is 0.91 at 100 m, 0.37 at 500 m, and 0.07 at 1,000 m below the observed edge. The deterioration is gradual: there is no five-bin switch in the prediction code. These results use 65,840 reporting-validation profiles at familiar stations, not the nearby radar as ground truth. Eligibility and profile composition differ across depths.

Each target bin is a separate prediction from the same observed upper profile. There is no smoothness constraint, boundary-matching constraint, or joint profile loss. As depth and target height change, tree thresholds can produce bends or jumps. Predictions are not recursively fed into the next bin, so this is not accumulated recursive error.

Deep layers are also less well represented: training contains about 2.95 million target rows at 100 m versus 0.77 million at 1,000 m. Training hides measured layers; operational application predicts naturally missing layers. This can change the distribution of terrain, coverage, and profile conditions. These are plausible contributors, not isolated causal findings.

The model predicts cube-root normalized density. Its output is cubed, clipped at zero, and multiplied by observed upper VID. Cubing can magnify changes in positive model output. Squared-error fitting on the transformed scale also does not directly optimize raw-density error. In paired-radar comparisons, the stations sample different airspace, so mismatches can additionally reflect real spatial or measurement differences. The “Upper agreement” tab addresses that concern.

How XGBoost feature importance works

Split count counts how often a feature appears in a tree split; it does not measure the size of its benefit. Gain measures improvement in the training objective from a split. Here we use total gain, summed across all splits using a feature, and divide by total gain across the entire model. XGBoost also offers average gain and cover; these answer different questions and can rank features differently.

The lowest observed bin (slot_00, after upper-VID normalization and cube-root transformation) contributes 39.5% of total training gain. Target height above the minimum-terrain proxy contributes 7.35%, depth below the observed edge 7.20%, and the next observed bin 5.58%. This is neither a percentage of explained variance nor a percentage of any individual prediction. Correlated inputs can substitute for one another, so the ranking is not a causal ranking.

What drives shallow versus deep predictions?

SHAP contributions decompose a particular model prediction into a baseline plus signed feature contributions. Positive contributions raise the prediction relative to that baseline; negative contributions lower it. Mean absolute SHAP summarizes contribution magnitude across selected rows, discarding direction. We use exact TreeSHAP from the saved booster, with training path cover as its background; no refitting is involved.

For these eight profiles, mean absolute depth contribution rises from 0.093 at bins 1–4 to 0.233 at bins 5–10 (about 2.5 times). Terrain-height contribution rises from 0.086 to 0.122; the lowest observed bin remains strongest (0.394 versus 0.370). Season and night-phase contributions also increase. These values are in the model’s transformed units, not birds/km³.

This is a deliberately small diagnostic sample: four evenly spaced timestamps from each existing KSOX and KMUX gallery, selected without consulting predictions, giving eight profiles and 76 target rows. All eight contribute to both depth groups; KMUX extends to ten bins and KSOX to nine. The rows are not independent, and the galleries may overlap model-development data. Do not interpret this ranking as a population estimate or an independent accuracy result.

Inspecting individual profile shapes

Read the density panels together with the contribution panels below. Each title identifies the exact timestamp and radar pair. Within a profile, observed slots, season, and night phase stay fixed; only depth and target height change. Contributions attributed to fixed inputs can still change because the model uses interactions with depth and height.

The grouped curves sum, together with the baseline, to the model output on the cube-root normalized scale. “Other upper bins” sums signed contributions across slots 1–28, so contributions within that group can cancel. These grouped curves are different from adding absolute importance scores. A large feature contribution does not by itself identify the source of an error; that requires reliable target measurements.

Do not cube each SHAP value separately. First sum the baseline and all contributions, then cube and multiply by upper VID. The transformation is nonlinear, so individual contributions are not additive in final density units. Upper VID is not a booster feature: it normalizes inputs and rescales the output, which means its role is not captured by a feature-importance bar.

What this supports, and what to check next

The evidence supports treating deep predictions as much less reliable than shallow predictions, and examining depth/terrain interactions alongside the lowest observed bin. It does not establish a universal five-bin cutoff or justify enforcing monotonically increasing or decreasing density: real profiles can have peaks.

An existing matched retraining experiment removed target AGL and worsened raw-density RMSE at every depth (about 3.8% at 500 m and 4.0% at 1,000 m). That argues against simply dropping AGL as a fix. AGL may carry both physical height information and site cues; the ablation does not distinguish them.

The next diagnostic should use a broader sample of held-out nights, stratified by depth and radar, and inspect the specific anomalous profiles with trustworthy reference measurements. Grouped permutation importance can measure the loss of validation skill when information is disrupted, but blindly shuffling normalized slots or correlated depth/height inputs creates unrealistic combinations. Matched feature-group retraining and physically valid sensitivity checks are better complements to SHAP. Any smoothing or joint-profile model should be judged on held-out profiles, not appearance alone.

Reproduction and checks

Model: conus-depth1to10-20261005-01, with AGL, all 10,000 trees. Inputs: 29 observed density slots, depth, terrain-relative target height, two night-phase terms and two seasonal terms. This is not the no-AGL or coordinates model.

Run from the repository root:

.venv-conus/bin/python analysis/depth-diagnostics/attribute.py
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("analysis/depth-diagnostics/report.Rmd", output_file="report.html")'
python3 scripts/build-radar-pair-tabs.py

Attribution is computed with Python XGBoost 3.2.0; all plots are produced in R with ggplot2 and ragg. CSVs, the attribution audit, R source, and standalone PNG figures are retained in analysis/depth-diagnostics/. Maximum SHAP reconstruction error is below 0.00001 in transformed units. The predictions also match the existing native-R gallery output to a maximum absolute difference of 1.41e-05 birds/km³.

Methods: XGBoost feature importance and prediction API and R prediction contributions. Source validation metrics: metadata/runs/conus-depth1to10-20261005-01-metrics.csv; matched AGL ablation: metadata/runs/conus-depth-agl-comparison-20261005.csv.
